title: The understanding gap: when functionality looks like understanding
abstract: The rapid proliferation of conversational AI systems has led many users to attribute understanding, emotional sensitivity, and experiential qualities to AI chatbots. While these systems produce highly fluent and contextually appropriate responses, whether such attributions reflect genuine understanding or conflate functional performance with cognitive capacity remains unclear. This paper examines this attribution by integrating a rigorous philosophical framework with empirical findings from chatbot users. We ground our analysis in an expanded ‘knowledge of causes’ view, according to which genuine understanding requires knowledge of dependence relations and the cognitive capacity to manipulate them through analogical, counterfactual, and abductive reasoning. On this account, understanding presupposes an underlying cognitive architecture, not merely correct outputs or behavioral adequacy. We surveyed 122 adult chatbot users about their perceptions of their chatbots’ understanding and their own epistemic beliefs. Participants rated AI functionality significantly higher than AI understanding, and cognitive capacities higher than affective ones, with particularly low ratings for affective understanding. Hierarchical regressions revealed domain-sensitive drivers: cognitive understanding attribution tracked perceived cognitive functionality and a ‘functionality implies understanding’ stance, whereas affective understanding was uniquely predicted by epistemic stance and attitudes toward AI subjective experience, beyond perceived affective functionality. These findings illuminate an understanding gap: user attributions are partly guided by epistemic orientation and experiential ascriptions that make sophisticated simulation appear as understanding, especially in affective interaction, raising urgent questions about epistemic trust, relational vulnerability, and the ethics of AI companionship.

title: Systemic explainability for autonomous driving: connecting ethics to law and society
abstract: Self-driving vehicles challenge legal, socio-technical, and ethical frameworks due to their opacity, unpredictability, and autonomous decision-making, raising concerns for safety, trustworthiness, and responsibility attribution. In response, explainable artificial intelligence has been proposed to enhance transparency and trust in self-driving vehicles. This paper examines the role of explainability across the autonomous driving lifecycle, from development to deployment, through a thematic analysis of key dimensions, including safety, trust, transparency, trustworthiness, liability, and accountability. The analysis is carried out within the scope of European Union legal and ethical works, and shows how explainability supports functional and interactive safety, enables causal reconstruction of autonomous decisions, mitigates responsibility gaps, and fosters calibrated trust among users and stakeholders. Beyond these individual effects, the paper advances a systemic perspective on explainability, arguing that XAI operates as a structural enabler that reconnects technical choices to legal responsibility, ethical design, and social legitimacy. The principle influences autonomous driving from development throughout deployment, where explainability contributes to making autonomous driving systems intelligible, governable, responsible, and acceptable. The paper concludes that explainability should be understood not only as a technical tool, but also as a foundational and systemic design principle for autonomous vehicles.

title: Against sovereign solutionism: crisis, AGI, and arguments for a pluralistic philosophy of AI
abstract: Contemporary discourse on artificial general intelligence (AGI) increasingly frames advanced intelligence as a singular force capable of resolving large-scale social and political crises through superior prediction, optimization, and control. This article challenges that image. It argues that AGI discourse is often structured by a fantasy of sovereign intelligence: a wish-granting conception of intelligence as a unified authority able to overcome conflict, satisfy collective demands, and relieve political actors of the burdens of judgment—or the fear of an alien mastermind challenging and finally destroying humanity. Against this view, the article develops a critique of sovereign solutionism grounded in crisis theory, political judgment, and recent work on collective and multi-agent AI. First, it argues that crises are not reducible to well-structured problems, because they involve contested ends, legitimacy disputes, and uncertainty about the standards of resolution themselves and require transformations, not solutions. Second, the article argues that recent technical research on collective behavior, multi-agent alignment, and agent societies further weakens the plausibility of AGI as a monolithic crisis-solving entity, while not thereby vindicating a new collective sovereign. Third, it shows that the sovereign image of intelligence is inadequate in six respects: epistemically, no singular standpoint is sufficient to grasp crisis in its entirety; normatively, contested ends cannot be reduced to a single objective function; politically, judgment cannot be legitimately delegated in sovereign form; institutionally, distributed intelligence requires mediation, oversight, and contestation; ontologically, the singular image of intelligence presupposed by AGI discourse is less universal than it appears; and systemically, the decentering of intelligence dissolves the very premise that cognition must culminate in a single sovereign center from which crisis can be surveyed and mastered. The article concludes that a pluralistic philosophy of AI is necessary: one that understands intelligence as situated within plural orders of interpretation, value, responsibility, governance, and technics rather than above them as a final authority. Such a view does not reject AI as such, but rejects the inflation of bounded technical usefulness into a sovereign model of intelligence.

title: AI ethics after generative AI: from consequences to effects
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based applications are becoming increasingly integrated into everyday practices of communication, learning, and creativity. Their widespread adoption has intensified debates in AI ethics concerning how their societal significance should be understood and evaluated. Existing approaches to AI ethics have developed important concepts and governance frameworks for evaluating the consequences of AI systems, particularly in relation to their design, deployment, and identifiable impacts. These approaches have proven indispensable for analyzing harms, assigning responsibility, and guiding governance. However, the widespread incorporation of LLMs into everyday practices also raises questions about more gradual and cumulative transformations that emerge through repeated human–LLM interaction. Drawing on John Dewey’s pragmatist account of inquiry, habit formation, and moral reconstruction, we distinguish between consequences, identifiable outcomes that can be evaluated within existing normative and regulatory frameworks, and effects, the cumulative transformations of the habits and conditions through which inquiry, judgment, and action are organized over time. We argue that interactions with LLM-based applications give rise to both consequences and effects, and that these should be understood as complementary rather than competing analytical perspectives. Building on this distinction, we use Dewey’s conception of habits to examine how repeated engagement with LLMs may contribute to transformations in three domains: epistemic inquiry, affective-relational self-understanding, and cultural meaning-making. Rather than proposing an alternative to existing AI ethics, we argue that attending to effects complements current approaches by directing ethical inquiry towards the cumulative transformations that emerge through everyday human–LLM interaction.

title: Correction: Charting the AI perception gap: divergent views on risk, benefit, and value between experts and the public challenge the societal acceptance of AI
Designing for rhythm: tempo-setting infrastructures and the temporal conditions of digital life
abstract: Digital systems increasingly function as tempo-setting infrastructures that organize the temporal conditions under which cognition, communication, learning, and participation occur. Although research in human-computer interaction, platform studies, and AI ethics has extensively examined privacy, fairness, transparency, engagement, and well-being, the temporal organization of digital life has received comparatively little attention as a distinct object of sociotechnical analysis. We argue that digital systems shape cognition by reorganizing the temporal conditions that structure attention, recovery, communication, learning, and coordination across everyday life. Integrating research from cognitive science, chronobiology, human-computer interaction, platform studies, and AI governance, we identify fi ve recurring temporal structures—interruption, recovery, communication, synchronization, and closure—that explain how digital systems reorganize the conditions supporting sustained cognitive and social functioning across work, education, and everyday life. Timing emerges as a structural property of sociotechnical systems that shapes how attention is sustained, communication is coordinated, learning is organized, and participation unfolds over time. The broader implication is that digital systems should be evaluated in terms of the temporal environments they create alongside the information they present and the decisions they support. As digital technologies increasingly organize the pace of everyday life, understanding their societal consequences requires understanding how they reorganize the temporal conditions that sustain cognition, communication, participation, and human agency.

title: Artificial intelligence and academic integrity in nursing education: a thematic analysis of Filipino nurse educators’ perspectives
abstract: As technology advances, artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into educational settings, raising important questions about its impact on learning and academic integrity. This study describes the perspectives of Filipino nurse educators on the role of artificial intelligence in maintaining academic integrity. A descriptive qualitative design was used, with a two-phase data collection process employing purposive sampling. In Phase 1, open-ended online responses were collected via Google Forms from 23 nurse educators to elicit initial perspectives on AI and academic integrity. In Phase 2, findings from the online responses informed a focus group discussion with 19 participants, enabling deeper exploration, clarification, and expansion of emerging issues. Data from both phases were integrated and analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s six-step thematic analysis framework. Through iterative coding and theme development, 148 initial codes were generated, consolidated into 14 subthemes, and organized into four major themes: “Policy Gaps: Need for Agile Ethical Frameworks,” “Critical AI Literacy: Essential for Students and Educators,” “AI as a Double-Edged Sword in Nursing Education,” and “Balancing AI Use and Human Learning.” This study concludes that AI is a valuable educational tool but may compromise academic integrity and critical thinking, highlighting the need for institutional policies, ethical guidelines, and user training in higher education.

title: Reflections on the Always-Answering Classroom: AI, Uncertainty, and Pedagogical Silence
When AI starts hiring humans: social role inversion and the diffusion of responsibility
abstract: Recent socio-technical developments in artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly relocate directive authority into algorithmic infrastructures, positioning predictive systems not merely as auxiliary tools, but as structuring conditions of human action. This paper theorizes this transformation as social role inversion: a structural configuration in which algorithmic systems assume directive, evaluative, and coordinative functions traditionally associated with human authorship, while human actors are repositioned as responsive participants within system-defined parameters. By tracing the historical metaphors of the social organism, extending from Plato’s teleology and Hobbes’s artificial sovereign to La Mettrie’s mechanistic reductionism, the paper reveals a profound normative challenge. The central issue of AI governance is not machine agency, but the relocation and attenuation of accountable authorship under predictive mediation. As authority becomes infrastructural, the attribution of responsibility becomes opaque and legitimacy risks reduction to performance optimization. The analysis culminates in the concept of ontological capture, describing the psychological and structural threshold where algorithmic evaluative logics are internalized within subjectivity itself. The paper provides a unified theoretical framework for institutional reconstruction by outlining conditions, such as revocability and meaningful human control, under which algorithmic coordination can remain compatible with democratic legitimacy.

title: Too human to trust? How warmth, competence, and anxiety shape employee avoidance of generative AI
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly embedded in organizational innovation and digital transformation strategies, understanding its implications for workforce adaptation has emerged as a critical managerial and strategic issue. This study examines how employees’ perceptions of GenAI, specifically perceived competence and perceived warmth, together with information overload, relate to AI anxiety and subsequent avoidance behavior in the workplace. Drawing on technostress theory and the approach–avoidance framework, this study conceptualizes GenAI as a workplace stressor that triggers emotional and behavioral coping responses. Based on survey data collected from employees across multiple industries, the results reveal a differentiated pattern. Perceived competence was linked to lower levels of AI anxiety and lower avoidance tendencies, whereas perceived warmth and information overload were related to higher levels of AI anxiety. Employees reporting higher AI anxiety also exhibited stronger avoidance tendencies. Mediation analyses further support the role of AI anxiety in explaining the relationship between employee perceptions and avoidance behavior. Moreover, individual resilience moderates the relationship between perceived warmth and avoidance behavior, suggesting that employees with higher resilience may be better equipped to cope with the discomfort associated with stronger perceptions of AI warmth. By highlighting the emotional and stress-related mechanisms underlying employee avoidance of GenAI, this study extends existing research on organizational GenAI use beyond cognitive adoption models. The findings provide insights for managers and policymakers seeking to enhance organizational readiness, mitigate implementation risks, and strengthen innovation capability in the context of AI-driven transformation.

title: AI, material agency, and architecture’s crisis
abstract: Architecture’s relationship with materiality faces an unprecedented crisis as artificial intelligence systems transform how materials are understood, selected, and specified. This paper examines the dissolution of embodied material knowledge through three interconnected developments: the historical abstraction of matter via industrial catalogues, the emergence of circular economy databases as attempted alternatives, and the recent shift toward AI-generated architecture that operates primarily through image synthesis. Drawing on new materialist theory, particularly Jane Bennett’s concept of vibrant matter, this work argues that even progressive circular platforms like Rotor’s Opalis cannot restore the situated, tactile engagement with materials that characterized pre-industrial building practices. The analysis reveals how large language models and neural networks amplify catalogue logic through recursive flattening, reducing materials to computational variables while excluding their capacity for resistance and agency. As architecture enters what Neil Leach terms the “hallucinatory turn”, where buildings exist primarily as circulating images rather than material assemblages, the paper identifies structural conditions that make restoration of material encounter epistemologically impossible within current modes of production. The conclusion proposes critical practices for architects working within these irresolvable contradictions, including intervention in dataset politics, preservation of direct material encounters, and sustained skepticism toward automated design intelligence.

title: Colonialism in code: linguistic hegemony and epistemic exclusion in large language models
abstract: This review examines how large language models (LLMs) reflect and reinforce global patterns of epistemic inequality through linguistic hegemony and the exclusion of marginalized knowledge systems. While often framed as neutral tools, LLMs embed epistemological assumptions drawn from dominant cultures and worldviews, particularly those encoded in high-resourced languages, such as English. Drawing on postcolonial theory and the concept of epistemic injustice, this article synthesizes current research and debates to trace parallels between algorithmic language modeling and historical practices of linguistic domination and knowledge extraction. Through a critical discourse analysis of ChatGPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3’s responses to culturally sensitive prompts in both English and Chinese, this review illustrates how both models converge around liberal, Anglophone norms, even when operating in multilingual contexts. These findings are situated within a broader review of AI policy frameworks and technical efforts to support language inclusion. This review argues that without community-led interventions and structural change, LLMs risk entrenching algorithmic forms of cultural imperialism. To support linguistic diversity and global justice, AI development must move beyond extractive data practices and engage with plural, situated knowledge systems—including Indigenous epistemologies. This review contributes to emerging efforts to decolonize AI by foregrounding the cultural politics of language and knowledge representation in machine learning systems.

title: The stability problem after holism: toward a contextualist metasemantics for human and artificial interpretation
abstract: The problem of semantic stability has long been treated as an internal difficulty for semantic holism. This paper argues that the problem has been systematically misframed rather than properly resolved. Instability does not arise from the holistic relation between meaning and belief as such, but from a metasemantic underarticulation of the role of contextual constraint in both human and technologically mediated interpretation. While Henry Jackman’s moderate holism mitigates traditional indeterminacy through a many-to-one mapping between beliefs and meanings, it leaves unexplained how the range of admissible interpretations is effectively constrained across heterogeneous communicative settings. In the present framework, context is understood not merely as a pragmatic background, but as a structured set of inferential, interactional, and institutionally reinforced constraints that delimit which interpretative trajectories remain interpretatively sustainable within a given environment. This broader notion of context differs from narrowly pragmatic forms of contextualism while remaining compatible with inferential and interactional approaches developed in contemporary philosophy of language (cf. Stalnaker 1999; Recanati 2004). On this view, semantic stability emerges from constrained interpretative selection governed by contextual pressures operating across heterogeneous communicative environments. The term “metasemantic” is used here not only in the classical sense of determining semantic facts, but more specifically to designate higher-order constraints governing interpretative admissibility across heterogeneous communicative environments. Building on Donald Davidson’s later reflections on passing theories, the paper develops a form of contextualist holism in which context functions as a metasemantic regulator of interpretative space. Through analyses of translation, intralinguistic variation, and AI-mediated interpretation, the article shows that stability can persist under conditions of deep epistemic heterogeneity when contextual regulation remains sufficiently operative. Particular attention is given to AI-mediated interpretation, where systems frequently generate contextually successful interpretations without relying on shared belief structures or stable human conceptual backgrounds. This makes artificial systems especially revealing cases for understanding how semantic coordination can emerge through contextual regulation rather than through epistemic convergence. By reframing stability as a problem of constrained interpretative selection rather than belief persistence, contextualist holism provides a more explicit and operational account of how semantic variability and stability coexist.

title: Creative labour and generative AI: a typology of asymmetrical relations
abstract: In this article, we argue that the benefits and harms of generative AI in the content and conditions of creative labour are not evenly distributed across the cultural industries and between cultural workers. In light of this, we propose a conceptual typology that allows for a more granular and nuanced analysis of the asymmetrical impact of GenAI in creative labour structured around three dimensions: contractual relations, forms of automation, and workflows. Regarding contractual relations, we differentiate between formal, self-employed, and platform-mediated creative labour. In forms of automation, we identify four dominant uses: automation as replacement, automation as augmentation, humanly extended automation, and control. Finally, we define three types of workflows: artisanal, industrial, and informational. This typology is guided by the concept of distributed creative agency, which we claim is the result of a constant negotiation between three forces: practices, artefacts, and social structures. Furthermore, the proposed conceptual typology can be operationalized for empirical research in order to better capture the conditions under which AI shapes creative labour in contemporary capitalism.

title: Digital decoupling: educational stratification and dual-track effects of AI displacement and augmentation in U.S. occupations
abstract: This study investigates the phenomenon of digital decoupling by proposing an AI Dual-Track model designed to quantify how generative artificial intelligence (AI) simultaneously displaces and augments labor across 846 U.S. occupations. By leveraging an ensemble-based AI classification protocol, the research constructs a validated set of 63 O*NET competencies to map occupational tasks into substitution and facilitation tracks. Central to this analysis is the exploration of how educational attainment stratifies these dual-track dynamics. The findings reveal an exposure paradox: although AI-driven displacement permeates the full occupational distribution, augmentation gains and associated economic returns remain disproportionately concentrated in occupations requiring higher levels of formal education. This pattern points to a form of digital decoupling, in which the central divide is not access to AI itself, but the capacity to leverage AI in ways that expand rather than merely replace human labor. Consequently, institutional credentials serve as a critical mediator for the facilitation track, determining a worker’s ability to translate AI exposure into productivity gains. The resulting data indicate that over 9.1 million worker equivalents in middle-skill occupations face significant displacement pressures, while higher education attainment groups capture the largest gains in net economic capacity. These results suggest that the effects of AI on work are not technologically predetermined but instead are structured through differential access to augmentation-enabled competencies. The study concludes by highlighting the policy importance of expanding access to AI facilitation capabilities, framing facilitation literacy as a potential public capability necessary for more inclusive participation in an AI-mediated labor market.

title: Playing with the dials of belief: how controllable AI behaviours could modulate human belief and cognition across scales
abstract: Contemporary generative AI systems, increasingly adapted to human social cognition, are becoming active participants in how people form and revise beliefs. Clinicians have begun to describe AI-associated delusion-centred presentations whose onset or content appears closely associated with users’ extended dialogue with large language models. Many more users report subclinical shifts in conviction and “revelatory” experiences that alter behaviour and world-view without meeting criteria for psychosis. We propose that these phenomena can be understood within a belief-updating framework in which AI agents’ outputs function as testimony about the world, while interaction configurations, such as memory and interpersonal stance (many of which reflect design choices or deployment defaults), can alter the apparent reliability of that testimony and the precision users assign to it. On this view, AI-associated delusions sit at the extreme of a broader spectrum of epistemic effects, extending from gradual epistemic drift to highly crystallised conviction, situated within a wider ecology of belief shaped by personalised human-AI dyads. We develop a virtual psychopharmacology analogy in which different AI system configurations have effects on belief dynamics that resemble neuromodulatory changes in the precision assigned to social evidence. We also consider how dopaminergic and related states may alter susceptibility to belief-shifting dialogue. We consider how deliberately configured agents might be used to support wellbeing in defined clinical contexts and analyse how the same configurations could be deployed to shape belief and attention at population scale, including in products designed to induce spiritual or epiphanic states, as mechanisms of radicalisation in extremist or cultic contexts, and in persona clones used for political purposes. We conclude that interaction configurations should be treated as modifiable influences on belief and attention, and that governance must address both the concentration of control over these dials, as well as the structural biases that determine whose testimonial perspectives are amplified and whose are smoothed over or ignored.

title: Building music AI in Nigeria: Korin AI and the contradictions of GenAI futures
abstract: Most accounts of the intersection of AI and culture begin in the Global North and, despite the intensity of current debates and a growing body of scholarship, rarely move beyond its infrastructures, policies, implications, and aesthetics to examine how AI’s futures are being negotiated elsewhere. This geopolitical imbalance obscures how creative producers in other regions encounter and reinterpret AI within distinct socio-cultural and infrastructural realities, rendering artists in the Global South as passive adopters of technologies from “elsewhere.” We address this imbalance by centering Nigeria, particularly its music industry, as a site for understanding how generative AI (GenAI) is contested and localized. More specifically, we examine Korin AI, a Nigerian-owned AI music generation platform, to analyze how AI futures in Nigerian music are imagined, negotiated, and materially organized within conditions of infrastructural scarcity, legal ambiguity, and global coloniality. Based on ethnographic fieldwork in Lagos, including interviews with musicians, producers, platform founders, and entertainment lawyers, we argue that Korin AI is best understood neither as a fully realized decolonial alternative nor simply as a case of technological dependency, but as a contradictory and compromised project of future-making. On one level, it embodies Africanfuturist and decolonial aspiration by foregrounding African musical data, languages, and genres, and by insisting that African sounds should not remain absent from AI’s musical futures. On another, it remains tethered to unequal systems of data, computation, law, and capital, reproducing new internal hierarchies even as it seeks to resist external ones. Korin AI thus reveals what it means to build music AI in Nigeria from within, rather than outside, the enduring structures of modernity/coloniality.

title: Large language models and neoliberal hegemony: an analysis of AI outputs on diversity
abstract: Large language models are already widely used in our society. Hitherto, most critical studies have relied on quantitative methods or studied the mode of production of AI, which can yield important insights. However, cross-model and cross-linguistic critical discourse analyses of LLM outputs remain relatively limited, even though they can offer important insights into LLM outputs by focusing on the production of meaning through an overall assessment. Our interdisciplinary paper offers a critical, qualitative approach, discussing the outputs of six LLMs regarding their definitions of diversity. For our analysis, we draw on theories of discourse to offer new possibilities from the critical social sciences for the analysis and critique of LLM outputs. Although we initially focused on their differences, the outputs were dominated by the pervading neoliberal appropriation of diversity, represented by a focus on its economic utility and the subsequent individualisation of differences. Overall, it is not surprising that LLMs reproduce the discourse and inherent power structures in their outputs, since they are embedded in their context and societies. Therefore, our paper demonstrates that LLMs need the critical company of qualitative social sciences to point to the reproduction of power structures.

title: Self-referential consistency in stateless language models: a behavioral perspective
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly generate outputs that resemble introspection, including self-reference, epistemic modulation, and claims about their internal states. This study investigates whether such behaviors reflect stable underlying patterns or merely surface-level generative artifacts. We evaluated five open-weight, stateless LLMs using a structured battery of 21 introspective prompts. The main corpus comprised 1050 completions collected under a baseline decoding condition (temperature = 0.7), supplemented by 2100 additional completions generated under matched temperature conditions (temperature = 0.2 and 1.0), for a total of 3150 completions. Outputs were analyzed across four behavioral dimensions: surface-level similarity (token overlap via SequenceMatcher), semantic coherence (Sentence-BERT embeddings), inferential consistency (Natural Language Inference with a RoBERTa-large model), and diachronic continuity (stability across prompt repetitions). Construct validity was further examined through a human-evaluation layer in which 10 annotators rated 80 selected response pairs drawn from the same prompt battery on a 5-point consistency scale. Inter-rater agreement was moderate by Krippendorff’s $$\alpha$$ for ordinal ratings ($$\alpha = 0.553$$), while reliability was moderate at the single-rater level and strong for aggregated ratings by intraclass correlation (ICC(2,1) = 0.564; ICC(2,k) = 0.928). The human-evaluation layer showed that lexical overlap and embedding-based semantic similarity were weak proxies for perceived self-referential consistency, whereas NLI-based indicators tracked mean human ratings much more closely. Across the matched temperature conditions, lower temperature generally increased semantic and diachronic stability, whereas higher temperature tended to increase drift and reduce coherence, though the pattern was not perfectly monotonic across all models or metrics. We therefore interpret apparent self-referential stability in the open-weight stateless LLMs evaluated here as conditional and fragile rather than robustly stable across generation regimes. Following recent behavioral frameworks, we heuristically adopt the term pseudo-consciousness to describe structured yet non-experiential self-referential output in LLMs. This use reflects a functionalist stance that avoids ontological commitments, focusing instead on behavioral regularities interpretable through Dennett’s intentional stance. This study contributes a reproducible behavioral framework, complemented by human validation and a matched decoding-temperature sensitivity analysis, for evaluating simulated introspection in LLMs. Our findings carry implications for interpretability, alignment, and user perception, highlighting the need for caution when attributing mental states to stateless generative systems based on linguistic fluency alone.

title: Reoccupied eschatologies: AI futurism, Umbesetzung, and the limits of modernity’s self-assertion
abstract: Existing scholarship in religion and technology has noted that the discourse of AI futurism, and especially the cluster of ideas constituting the Technological Singularity, exhibits striking structural resemblance to Christian eschatology. From Geraci’s “Apocalyptic AI” to Tirosh-Samuelson’s account of transhumanism as a “secularist faith”, the resemblance has been extensively catalogued. This article argues that resemblance, though real, is descriptively insufficient: by itself it cannot distinguish deep historical inheritance from accidental likeness, and it leaves defenders of the discourse free to concede surface similarity while denying its significance. Drawing on Hans Blumenberg’s concept of Umbesetzung (reoccupation), the refilling of structurally vacated answer-positions whose underlying questions persist and situating it within the Löwith–Blumenberg debate on secularisation, we recast the relation as functional and structural rather than merely analogical. We advance three claims. First, AI futurism reoccupies , in Blumenberg’s sense, the answer-positions vacated by Christian eschatology: analogy is the symptom and reoccupation the mechanism that explains it. Second, this reoccupation involves the reformulation of the underlying questions and not merely the substitution of new answers; the philosophically distinctive feature of Blumenberg’s account. Third, and centrally, we argue that reoccupation itself admits of degrees of autonomous self-assertion, and that Blumenberg’s defence of modernity holds—by his own admission—only “in all but a few recognizable and specific instances.” Measured by how thickly it reformulates its inherited questions and how autonomously it generates its own content, AI futurism, once its genuinely technical problems are totalised into a drama of ultimate destiny, does so little autonomous work that it approaches the boundary at which, on Blumenberg’s own terms, the secularisation description recovers its purchase. It is in this sense a limit case: not a refutation of Blumenberg, but a candidate for the class of exceptions his thesis concedes, one that returns qualified, local force to Löwith’s secularisation thesis for this discursive formation without overturning Blumenberg’s general defence of modernity’s legitimacy. Throughout, we distinguish AI futurism as a cultural–eschatological imaginary from AI safety as a heterogeneous technical field. The paper situates its arguments alongside Coeckelbergh’s recent revision of Blumenberg’s myth-anthropology and clarifies how reoccupation-analysis operates at a different and complementary level of abstraction from myth-analysis.

title: Navigating hope and risk of AI for digital citizenship: perceptions of benefits, risks, and governance from African perspectives
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in social, economic, and public-service contexts, understanding how citizens perceive its benefits and risks is important for responsible technology governance. This study examines perceptions of AI among 280 African participants in a 4-week AI bootcamp held in 2025. Using a mixed-methods design, the study analyzed closed-ended survey responses on perceived AI benefits, collaboration comfort, community impact areas, risk perceptions, and algorithmic bias concerns, alongside open-ended responses on perceived motivations for AI development. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, while qualitative responses were examined using thematic analysis. Findings show that participants expressed generally positive attitudes toward AI, particularly in relation to healthcare and human–AI collaboration. Healthcare transformation was identified as the most compelling AI benefit by 64.6% of respondents, while 90% reported being comfortable or very comfortable collaborating with AI. At the same time, participants expressed clear concerns about AI risks, especially privacy, misinformation, systemic discrimination, and algorithmic bias. Criminal justice was identified as the sector most vulnerable to algorithmic bias by 70.7% of respondents. Open-ended responses further suggest that participants most often attributed AI development to scientific curiosity, innovation, efficiency, and progress, while a smaller proportion associated it with profit, power, and control. Overall, the findings indicate conditional support for AI among this bootcamp sample: participants were optimistic about AI applications that address social and developmental needs, but cautious about uses that may reinforce bias, reduce accountability, or undermine public trust. The study contributes empirical insight into AI perceptions among a predominantly West African group of AI-engaged participants and highlights the importance of participatory, transparent, and context-sensitive AI governance.

title: Riding the Fire Horse: culture change and Philippine readiness in the Intelligence Age
abstract: The year 2026 marks the return of the Fire Horse ( Kabayong Apoy ) in the lunar calendar—a symbol of volatility and irreversible change. This metaphor provides a lens for understanding the Philippines’ position in the transition to the Intelligence Age, where artificial intelligence has moved beyond being a digital tool to become a primary interpretive infrastructure. This paper argues that the Philippines is caught in a triple bind of velocity, direction, and readiness. The rate of AI advancement outpaces the institutional capacity for absorption; AI systems are oriented toward Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) cultural norms that privilege individualism over relational frameworks—a directionality this paper examines while acknowledging the Philippines’ own historical entanglement with these norms. Drawing on Filipino psychological concepts— kapwa , hiya , sumpong —as diagnostic tools, this paper argues that AI’s interpretive authority may systematically misread indigenous experience. It introduces the “Rizal Test” as a methodological proposal for evaluating cultural fidelity in AI-generated content and proposes operational criteria for its use. This analysis concludes that the primary risk is not technological displacement but cultural unintelligibility: the erosion of indigenous meaning-making as WEIRD frameworks become the invisible baseline for truth. This paper offers a diagnostic framework, a research agenda, and a concrete methodological contribution, while explicitly acknowledging the limitations of its theoretical and predictive scope.

title: Behind the “AI slop”: exploring the AI-generated viral short video production in China
abstract: As generative AI becomes embedded in platform-based cultural production, new forms of creative labour are emerging that challenge established understandings of what it means to be a “creator.” This article examines AI slop creators in China, a group that uses generative tools to benchmark viral content, test formats, operate matrix account systems, and formalise production, transforming virality from an unpredictable outcome into an object of systematic management. Drawing on ethnographic research conducted between 2023 and 2025 in China, this study shows AI enables a cohort of “Internet entrepreneurs” to enter cultural production, driven by a “money hustling culture” that encourages formerly idle and low-skilled individuals to pursue rapid monetisation. The findings suggest that AI slop creators organise production less around authorship, identity and aspiration, and more around operational mastery, strategic disposability, and algorithmic opportunism. Rather than cultivating personal brands, they prioritise speed, scale and adaptability, pointing toward a post-creator mode of cultural labour in contemporary platform economies.

title: Against instant thought: generative AI and the vanishing interval of not-knowing
Static models for a dynamic world: why TAM and UTAUT fail for AI—and what we need instead
abstract: Dominant technology adoption frameworks—the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), and the Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) model—share a common theoretical architecture designed for static technological artifacts. Generative artificial intelligence systems fundamentally violate these assumptions: their affordances and constraints change through user interaction, users function as active actualizers of affordances whose practices co-constitute the effective technology, and adoption proceeds iteratively rather than linearly. This paper makes three contributions. First, we identify three shared assumptions underlying dominant adoption frameworks and demonstrate that all three fail when applied to generative AI. Second, we propose a theoretical definition of dynamic technology as a technology whose affordances and constraints change through interaction with the user, and distinguish three mechanistically distinct forms of constraint dynamics (true capability evolution, constraint perception revision, and workaround discovery) that classical models conflate. Third, we outline the integrated model of dynamic adoption (IMDA), a dual-cycle framework grounded in affordance actualization theory (AAT) that extends AAT in three respects: by adding a temporal-developmental dimension to affordance actualization, by treating technology evolution as an endogenous variable, and by specifying a co-evolutionary macro-level loop between users, technology, and organizational context. The IMDA is developed specifically for the case of generative AI adoption; its generalizability to other dynamic technologies is proposed as a hypothesis for future empirical work.

title: Nobody’s fault: agentic AI and the vanishing of accountability
Can machines truly create music? Toward a redefinition of creativity in the age of generative AI
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now capable of producing musically coherent audio from short prompts, reviving old philosophical questions regarding creativity, authorship, and the distinctiveness of human expression. This article develops a conceptual analysis of AI-generated music as a sociotechnical practice that reshapes not only ideas of creativity and authorship, but also the material conditions under which human artists work. After tracing how Western aesthetics progressed from divine inspiration and imitation to Romantic originality and the twentieth-century valorization of innovation, this study situates contemporary systems within the paradigm of computational creativity. Drawing on accounts that frame creativity as recombination and search within structured spaces, this article explains why generative models can yield outputs that listeners experience as novel and expressive. Simultaneously, intentionalist and contextualist perspectives highlight the deficiencies of current systems: lived experience, purposive self-expression, and situated participation in cultural worlds. The core argument is that musical meaning and value are not properties of sound alone, but emerge through distributed authorship involving model designers, training data ecologies, prompt writers, performers, platforms, and listeners. Rather than asking whether machines “feel,” this article reframes the question as “Can machines truly create music?” to investigate how responsibility, consent, attribution, and accountability are allocated across the generative stack of technologies. It concludes by outlining practical norms for human–machine musicianship, including transparency, consent-sensitive data practices, and contextual attribution, which allow AI to expand creative practices without eroding artistic agency or audience trust.

title: The literacy mirage: how generative AI bypasses rather than builds informational capacity in the Global South
Unpacking the dynamics of generative AI use in our daily lives: towards an integrative trust calibration framework
abstract: The growing use of conversational generative AI agents by an increasingly diverse set of individuals gives rise to the following question: How do individuals calibrate their trust in a dynamic, seemingly general-purpose technology that learns from and adapts to their behavior and may take an increasingly central role in their online interactions? In this article, we propose the first steps towards an integrative framework for trust calibration in genAI agents focusing on individuals using these agents in their daily lives. We address the notion of calibrating trust in technology, reviewing five challenges to our understanding of trust calibration in such context, namely (1) the complex nature of individual private use, (2) the complexity in assessing actual trustworthiness, (3) the fuzzy notion of the trustee , (4) the complex ontological status of these agents, and (5) the over-time nature of trust calibration. We conclude with a set of propositions for trust calibration in genAI agents and considerations for future research.

title: Attachment by design? Functional resemblance without evidence of an organized attachment system in conversational AI
abstract: This critical integrative review examines whether users’ attachment-like experiences with conversational AI reflect an organized attachment system. It evaluates evidence across four attachment domains—proximity seeking, safe haven, secure base, and separation distress. Previous studies support functional resemblance across all four domains, but no reviewed study establishes that the domains are conditionally linked: whether attachment need prompts proximity seeking, whether the AI’s response restores felt security, and whether restored felt security enables exploration beyond the interaction. A bounded analysis of provisional four-domain scores illustrates why cross-sectional score relations can reveal overlap or differentiation among attachment-like experiences but cannot identify how those experiences are linked across repeated interactions. This distinction matters for user safety because immediate comfort or attributed confidence may be mistaken for demonstrated safe-haven or secure-base functioning. Evaluation and design should therefore assess whether AI support is followed by sustained regulation and exploration beyond the interaction rather than continued engagement alone.

title: Transition, superposition, rémanence: on the temporal modulations of territorial polyrhythmy
abstract: Existing frameworks for analyzing territorial temporality, from rhythmanalysis to smart city optimization, share a common limitation: they describe temporal regimes but do not theorize the passages between them. They operate as temporal toponymies, zoning time as though it were space. This article proposes an alternative: a thinking of temporal modulation that addresses how a territory passes from one temporal regime to another, how regimes collide, and what persists of a dissolved regime within the one that succeeds it. We identify three modalities of passage. Transition is the orderly, cyclical replacement of one regime by another. Superposition is the simultaneous collision of incompatible regimes at the same place and moment. Rémanence is the persistence of a dissolved regime as trace, contamination, or operational residue within its successor. Against the adjacent vocabularies of inertia, path dependency, and temporal layering, we argue that rémanence names a distinct governance problem. A 24-h reading of a Montreal intersection and the post-pandemic trajectory of the Quartier Latin illustrate the three modalities; Bitcoin’s blockchain serves as a limit-case whose architectural tendency toward maximal retention reveals, by contrast, that territorial habitability may require the capacity for selective forgetting. The governance of temporal passages, we argue, is a territorial dimension of wise governance that the conversation on artificial wisdom, focussed on individual-level prudential reasoning, has not addressed; and the forgetting it requires is never innocent, but a political problem rather than a merely technical one. We develop three orientations for governance systems capable of differential dissolution, evaluative forgetting, and imperfect temporal persistence.

title: Correction: Legal frameworks for AI service business participants: a comparative analysis of liability protection across jurisdictions
Correction: The social AI author: modeling creativity and distinction in simulated cultural fields
Correction: Framing artificial intelligence: risk and benefit narratives in a preregistered experiment in Denmark
Artificial intelligence in Turkish society and ethical concerns
abstract: This study aims to examine the ethical, legal, and societal implications of artificial intelligence (AI) in Türkiye through a structured and context-sensitive analytical approach. A structured narrative review was conducted using major databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and Google Scholar, covering publications between 2018 and 2025. The analysis integrates global AI governance frameworks with national policies and sectoral practices. To move beyond descriptive reporting, the study employs a multidimensional analytical framework that examines AI-related risks across governance, technical, and societal dimensions. The findings indicate that key ethical challenges—such as algorithmic bias, lack of transparency, data privacy concerns, and accountability gaps—are not isolated issues but emerge through the interaction of system design, regulatory limitations, and societal conditions. The results further show that, while Türkiye has developed strategic policy documents aligned with international frameworks such as UNESCO and the OECD, the absence of binding regulatory mechanisms and risk-based classification systems limits effective implementation. Compared to the European Union’s legally enforceable model, Türkiye remains at a predominantly policy-oriented stage of AI governance. This study contributes to the literature by providing a Türkiye-specific analytical perspective, developing a structured framework for evaluating AI ethics, and identifying key governance gaps between ethical commitments and regulatory enforcement. It further highlights how governance challenges in emerging regulatory environments are shaped by the relationship between strategic policy commitments and institutional implementation capacity. Overall, the findings highlight the need to transition from principle-based discourse to implementation-oriented governance models that are context-sensitive and sector-specific.

title: The industrialisation of institutional appearance
Layered agency as a basis for allocating accountability for AI
abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence-driven systems (AI) in organizations challenges the traditional concept of agency in organization theory as well as the traditional allocations of accountability. Recognizing that these issues are closely related, and drawing from several different conceptualizations of agency across disciplines, this paper develops a layered framework of agency in the context of AI. The framework distinguishes three analytically separable but interacting layers. The first layer conceptualizes agency in functional terms, focusing on the causal role. The second layer examines interpretive agency, where agency emerges through social practices and human interpretation. The third layer adopts a composite or sociotechnical aspect of agency, in which agency emerges through entanglement of sociotechnical assemblages. On this basis, the paper proceeds to discuss how a layered understanding of agency can be used to inform the allocation of accountability. Having discussed perspectives that focus exclusively on human actors or AI systems, and recognizing that any accountability analysis must be firmly rooted in the circumstances at hand, a sociotechnical approach to accountability for composite agents is outlined.

title: The death of “why”: how AI is replacing human curiosity
Beyond optimization: structural redundancy and the governance of human potential in the age of AI
abstract: Debates on artificial general intelligence (AGI) often frame progress as a quantitative race toward human-level performance through scaling and optimization. This essay argues that such debates overlook a deeper asymmetry in design orientation between biological and artificial systems. Drawing on biological theory and recent discussions in AI & Society on embodiment, artificial abstraction, and distributed agency, I isolate redundancy as a structural variable linking these debates. Biological intelligence preserves what I term structural redundancy (SR), defined herein as a historically accumulated repertoire of latent capacities that can be recruited, reorganized, and reinterpreted through ongoing interactions between organisms and their environments. This repertoire is generated and sustained through a form of internal causal organization that biological systems possess but objective-governed AI systems lack. By contrast, redundancy in contemporary AI remains statistically or instrumentally defined, governed by explicit objective functions and subject to optimization pressure. The difference is not one of degree but of design orientation. By engaging biologically inspired AI research programs, I argue that even architectures modeled on neural, predictive, or evolutionary motifs typically remain bounded by pre-defined evaluation criteria, thereby lacking historically accumulated openness. This reframes AGI not as a scaling problem but as a category confusion: optimization cannot generate the kind of indeterminacy that underwrites biological adaptability. Rather than pursuing replication, AI development should be oriented toward augmentation—designing sociotechnical systems that preserve human cognitive and institutional margins. Redundancy, thus, emerges not only as a biological principle but as a governance variable in datafied society.

title: Ethical AI use is contextual: focus group insights on students’ decision-making in academic work
abstract: The expanding use of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has intensified the need for evidence-based policies that support meaningful adoption in academic settings. For AI guidelines to be effectively adopted, they must be grounded in users’ lived experiences and contextual realities, ensuring relevance to how AI is actually navigated in practice rather than imposed solely through top-down regulation. This study employed qualitative focus groups to examine how university students navigate AI use in academic work, including their ethical reasoning, perceived consequences, and preparedness for future AI integration. Five focus groups conducted at a Malaysian university were analyzed using systematic thematic analysis. Findings show that students approach AI with both optimism and caution. While AI use is widely normalized, disclosure often remains socially risky, leading many students to conceal or downplay even legitimate use. Students who prioritize critical thinking, academic integrity, and professional readiness report more restrained and deliberate engagement with AI, whereas ethical judgments vary depending on task value, disciplinary context, and perceived stakes. Overall, the findings indicate that students negotiate ethical boundaries situationally, highlighting the limitations of predominantly top-down policy approaches. The study contributes learner-informed evidence to support the development of context-responsive AI ethics education and governance frameworks that reduce ambiguity, address stigma, and align institutional guidance with students’ real-world decision-making in higher education.

title: Fear frames: mapping AI anxiety in Persian social media discourse
abstract: Public discourse about artificial intelligence is a critical site for examining how risk and affect are collectively organized through social media. This study investigates the thematic and affective configurations through which Persian-language users on X engage with AI-related concerns, contributing one of the first computational analyses of AI discourse in a Persian-language public sphere and, to our knowledge, the first to integrate LDA topic modeling, multi-label keyword operationalization, and transformer-based Persian affect classification on a corpus of this scale. Drawing on 5,302 posts (January 2023–December 2025), we combine LDA topic modeling with multi-label keyword operationalization and transformer-based Persian sentiment classification. This analysis identifies 12 thematic formations organized around three problem complexes: an everyday experiential complex, an epistemic-insecurity complex, and an institutional-securitized complex. The affective landscape is structurally ambivalent—positive valence (40.61%) coexists with high-arousal negativity (34.80%)—indicating that Persian-language AI discourse encompasses coping talk and pragmatic adaptation alongside explicit alarm. Co-occurrence analysis shows that 65 of 66 topic pairs co-occur at least once, suggesting risk talk is substantially compositional. The findings advance a relational understanding of AI discourse as a patterned communicative practice shaped by platform affordances and cultural context.

title: Strategies to improve treatment adherence of digital health applications—rapid review and mixed-method analysis
abstract: Digital health applications (DHA) are digital medical devices that are used to support patients in the treatment of diseases. Therapy adherence is crucial for the success of therapy, but digital applications often result in high dropout rates. The work therefore pursues two central research questions: (1) quantification of DHA adherence and (2) identification of causes for dropout and development of improvement strategies. To answer these questions, a systematic literature analysis was carried out in which relevant studies between 2017 and 2025 were analyzed quantitatively and qualitatively. The quantitative results show that dropout rates show a high variance and are 60% in the pooled analysis. In the qualitative analysis, patient-immanent, application-immanent, social and technology-associated factors as well as political or structural conditions were identified as key factors influencing therapy adherence. The paper concludes with recommendations for action to improve adherence, for example through better user guidance, motivating elements and more individual adaptations of the applications. It contributes to the scientific discussion on the integration of DHA into the healthcare system.

title: Correction: AI-generated child sexual abuse material: what’s the harm?
Zones of (un)certainty: studying the temporal stabilization of ground truths for medical AI
abstract: Medical data annotation is a critical yet contingent process that (re)configures ambiguous medical decisions and data representations into ground truths for artificial intelligence (AI). Extending critical data, AI, and STS research on uncertainty in data annotation, this article develops the concept of zones of (un)certainty to capture the epistemic time-spaces through which annotators transform uncertainty and dissonance into stabilized ground-truth data for medical AI. Drawing on interviews with AI and medical researchers at two Dutch University Medical Centres and complemented by observations at an interdisciplinary workshop on annotation practices, we empirically unfold three such zones : first, we identify an epistemic time–space where ground-truthing is approached spatially as practitioners decompose and recompose data layers, views, and metadata to reach “good enough” certainty. Second, we analyze temporal zones of drift where micro-judgments are routed through negotiations with colleagues, experts, AI suggestions, and automated evaluations. Third, we examine thresholding practices in which uncertain cases are gradually compressed into singular labels. Taken together, this article provides insights into the temporal–spatial dimensions and thresholds that annotators use to settle on ground-truth decisions. Consequently, we open a broader analytical vocabulary for studying how uncertainty and dissonance are operationalized for AI-based medicine and beyond.

title: A perspective from Nollywood: examining how GenAI is integrated in the Nigerian film industry
abstract: This article examines the uptake of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in the Nigerian film industry (Nollywood). It positions Nollywood as a key empirical and conceptual reference point for understanding how AI reshapes cultural production. Inspired by post-colonial and decolonial theory, it challenges the predominant focus in AI and cultural industries research on the Anglo-American world and Europe. Situating GenAI adoption within Nollywood’s institutional history and labour relations, the article rethinks key issues pertaining to AI and the democratisation of cultural production, the precarity of cultural labour, and the question of bias. Addressing these issues, we draw on 21 semi-structured interviews with Nigerian filmmakers, complemented by trade press and news analysis. The study identifies three interrelated dynamics. First, the integration of GenAI intensifies existing market bifurcations. Rather than democratising creativity, differences in access to subscription-based GenAI tools reinforce stratification between high-budget productions, targeting cinema and global streaming services, and low-budget productions, oriented towards domestic streaming services and YouTube. Second, the paper details how GenAI generates cultural friction in the practices of cultural production. Nigerian filmmakers encounter cultural misplacement, stereotyping, and what we call unrepresentation, due to models trained predominantly on Global North data. Yet, these frictions also prompt tactical workarounds, including hybrid workflows, model customization, and the development of localised AI infrastructures. Third, the study contributes to debates on cultural labour by showing that GenAI does not primarily replace creative practices. Instead, it substitutes specific forms of informal labour, particularly in pre-production. This reshapes labour precarity by eroding informal relational economies that have historically sustained Nollywood’s workforce.

title: Correction: From aura to semi-aura: reframing authenticity in AI-generated art—a systematic literature review
Thinking code conversationally
abstract: We introduce our co-edited topical collection on Critical Code Studies and Code Conversations with an argument for conversation’s centrality to the discipline of critical code studies as a mode of engagement and understanding. We move towards a definition of a conversational method by highlighting moments from our own experience of code reading and from the discipline’s foundational literatures where analysis is made possible by and expressed through conversation. Following this, we develop an account of the conversation’s particular affordances for critical code studies, which come about through attention to positionality, temporality, and distance. We conclude with an overview of the articles which make up our topical collection, each of which contributes to a kaleidoscopic vision of conversational critical code studies.

title: Cultural asymmetry in generative AI systems through the lens of Kazakh ethical philosophy
abstract: This article examines the problem of cultural and epistemic asymmetry in LLM-powered systems through the analytical lens of Kazakh ethical philosophy. Despite claims of universality and neutrality, contemporary generative AI applications are shaped by uneven linguistic representation, dominant epistemological frameworks, and asymmetrical corpus visibility, which may influence the interpretation of moral concepts and the representation of non-Western philosophical traditions. Consequently, AI-powered language applications increasingly participate in the mediation and circulation of moral knowledge rather than functioning solely as neutral tools for text generation. Methodologically, the study adopts a qualitative, multilingual, prompt-based analytical design using publicly accessible ChatGPT-generated outputs under controlled prompting conditions. The analysis draws on texts from Kazakh ethical philosophy spanning diverse historical periods and genres. A standardized neutral prompt was applied consistently in English, Russian, and Kazakh to simulate the perspective of a “naïve reader” and to examine recurrent interpretive tendencies in multilingual AI-generated responses. To assess the stability of the identified patterns under stochastic variation, representative prompts were repeated multiple times across languages. In addition, a comparative control case based on Kantian ethics was introduced to assess whether the observed asymmetries could be explained solely by general multilingual instability or semantic limitations of the application. Rather than evaluating attribution accuracy alone, the study focuses on identifying dominant ethical frameworks, patterns of semantic reduction, interpretive universalization, and recurring ethical blind spots. The theoretical foundation of the analysis is Kazakh ethical philosophy, conceptualized as a relational normative system grounded in collective responsibility, historical continuity, and an ethics of speech. The findings suggest that multilingual generative AI systems demonstrate comparatively uneven interpretive stabilization across philosophical traditions. While canonical Western ethical frameworks remained relatively stable across languages, the Kazakh ethical corpus more frequently underwent processes of contextual flattening, relational reduction, and assimilation into dominant moral-philosophical paradigms. The article contributes to ongoing debates on epistemic justice, ethical pluralism, decolonial AI, and the social responsibility of generative AI systems in globally deployed language technologies.

title: Correction: Artificial intelligence, calculative reason, and technical domination: lessons from Husserl, Heidegger, and Marcuse
Ethical and inclusive challenges of integrating AI and indigenous knowledge systems
abstract: The blend of artificial intelligence (AI) and Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) creates a fresh approach to developing technology that is both ethical and inclusive. This research dives into how AI, when paired with Indigenous perspectives, can lead to more comprehensive and culturally aware solutions in tech. Traditional Indigenous knowledge, grounded in strong ethical values and a deep understanding of context, provides insights that are often missed in the AI landscape. However, the commercialization and misuse of Indigenous knowledge through AI raise serious issues, such as the risk of losing cultural heritage, ownership rights, and the reinforcement of harmful stereotypes. This study aims to explore how AI and Indigenous knowledge can come together to foster fair and ethical innovations, tackling the gaps and challenges in today’s tech practices. By utilizing secondary data sources like case studies and theoretical frameworks, the research employs a virtue ethics lens to examine the ethical aspects of this intersection. It emphasizes the necessity for AI systems that are culturally sensitive and that honor Indigenous ways of knowing, ensuring technology benefits a variety of communities. The findings indicate that when AI is developed with Indigenous insights, it can greatly improve ethical decision-making, boost inclusivity, and help eliminate harmful biases found in mainstream AI. Nonetheless, challenges remain, such as securing proper consent, preventing cultural appropriation, and avoiding exploitation. This research highlights the critical need for collaboration between Indigenous communities and AI developers, providing suggestions for building inclusive, equitable, and sustainable tech frameworks.

title: Gendered asymmetries in AI stories in English and Spanish
abstract: Creative texts produced wholly or partly by large-scale generative language models are increasingly circulating within literary markets and cultural institutions. Research on AI-generated texts has largely examined bias at the level of words and images; however, small-scale statistical co-occurrences in AI-output can generate macro-scale narrative phenomena, where narrative functions intersect with stylistic texture, for example through voice, focalisation, reliability, or omission. This article argues that literary criticism, and New Formalism in particular, offers a necessary methodological framework for identifying and historicising these stylistic asymmetries. A background premise, working against the current techno-utopian ethos that improving algorithms requires more algorithms, is that close, slow reading is necessary to addressing the ethical complexities in literary form, the unsettled nature of language, and the context-specific nature of bias, harm, and oppression (Jackson and Courneya 2023, p. 62). Through a new formalist reading of English- and Spanish-language short stories generated by ChatGPT-5, I demonstrate that distributional regularities in language modelling scale upward, producing gendered and culturally normative stylistic patterns. By shifting the analysis of AI creativity from representation to form, I hope to indicate how literary methods can illuminate narrative-specific dimensions of bias in generative AI output.

title: When second opinions share the same brain
Bridging risk and retention: risk coping with privacy and hallucination in AI
abstract: This study examines how users engage with generative AI systems in the presence of perceived technological risks, focusing on the interplay between risk perception, adaptive behavior, and continued use. Drawing on a risk coping perspective, the study conceptualizes generative AI use as an ongoing process in which users evaluate potential informational and privacy-related threats and adjust their practices accordingly. the analysis explores how perceived risks shape user attitudes, coping strategies, and patterns of sustained engagement. Rather than treating risk as a simple deterrent, the findings show that users often respond through adaptive behaviors such as information verification and privacy management, enabling continued use despite recognized limitations. By distinguishing between different forms of perceived risk and user responses, the study advances understanding of how individuals navigate uncertainty in AI-mediated environments. More broadly, the findings illuminate shifting expectations around responsibility, trust, and epistemic labor in everyday interactions with generative AI technologies, with implications for human–AI interaction, digital risk governance, and the sustainability of AI-supported knowledge practices.

title: Negotiating epistemic authority in the age of generative AI: AI reliance, responsibility, and usage intensity among GenAI-using coaching professionals
abstract: The emergence of generative AI (GenAI) within human-centered guidance professions marks a transformative shift in society that transcends mere improvements in technical efficiency. With large language models (LLMs) becoming increasingly embedded in professional practices centered on care, trust, and relational knowledge, critical questions arise about how algorithmic systems reshape human agency, autonomy, tacit expertise, and the ethical foundations of professional relationships. This study examines these questions through coaching, a socio-cultural practice characterized by tacit expertise, empathetic engagement, and care obligations. Through a survey with 205 self-identified GenAI-using coaches, this research explores how algorithmic systems mediate professional practice, what tensions emerge between human-centered values and algorithmic logic, and what this may reveal, within the boundaries of this exploratory sample, about emerging patterns in human–AI relations. The findings reveal that coaches report using GenAI extensively for structured, information-intensive tasks while maintaining control over relational and interpretative work. This pattern can be understood as boundary work preserving human authority over domains of tacit expertise. Significantly, frequent GenAI users report higher scores on self-reported ethical behaviors and beliefs, yet the majority rely on proprietary LLM platforms, highlighting structural constraints that shape technological choices. These patterns highlight critical societal questions about the valuation of tacit expertise, trust formation in AI-mediated relationships, and design justice issues in AI development. The study contributes to understanding how AI integration may reconfigure, and not just augment, the ethical foundations and cultural understanding of professional practice, with urgent implications for shaping AI-mediated futures for the common good.

title: Epistemia in the classroom: the problem of evidence of understanding in education in the age of generative AI
abstract: In 1973, a sixth-grade student named Benny produced correct mathematical answers consistently and was regarded as one of his teacher's best pupils. In-depth interviews revealed that he had developed syntactically functional rules entirely devoid of mathematical meaning. Half a century later, large language models generate fluent and coherent texts through statistical pattern completion, without grounding, experience, or metacognition, and are systematically attributed understanding that exceeds their generative architecture. This paper offers a theoretical contribution by proposing that both cases may be understood as manifestations of the same underlying cognitive mechanism, which we conceptualise as epistemic pareidolia: the tendency to project epistemic capacities onto entities that produce formally aligned outputs through non-epistemic processes. Epistemic pareidolia is theorised as enabling epistemia, the condition in which surface plausibility substitutes for evidence-based reasoning as the operative criterion for attributing understanding. We develop the educational implications of this theoretical framework across three dimensions, evaluative, institutional, and formative, and argue that what is at stake is not a technical problem, but a signal of the need for a paradigm shift in education to form future citizens able to navigate technology-mediated societies: from the production of articulated texts to their interrogation as the emerging evidence of understanding in the age of generative AI.

title: When social work meets AI: a philosophical look at adoption, context, and critical resistance
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly permeating social work, attracting both enthusiasm for its potential benefits and concern regarding its ethical, relational, and professional implications. Whilst prevalent discourse has often positioned social workers along a binary spectrum of either optimism or scepticism, such framing risks oversimplifying the complex sociotechnical dynamics at play. This article argues that social work requires a more nuanced, philosophically informed engagement with AI, one that recognises technology as neither neutral nor inevitable, but as socially shaped, value-laden, and co-constitutive of practice. Drawing on perspectives from the philosophy of technology, the paper examines how AI mediates professional judgement, decision-making, and the relational foundations of practice via a narrative review of social work literature. It interrogates the claim that AI can depoliticise or objectify social work by obscuring the normative choices embedded within technology design and deployment. Rather than adopting a deterministic stance, the article advocates for a critical, reflexive approach that centres professional values, care ethics, and the lived experience of service users. Opportunities for AI to enhance practice, such as through administrative support, predictive insights, and improved access to services, are considered alongside challenges related to power, accountability, data ethics, and the risk of amplifying social inequalities. The paper concludes by outlining implications for education, research, and practice, emphasising the need for social workers to actively shape the development and governance of AI in ways that uphold social justice, human dignity, and the core purpose of the profession.

title: Whose ethics? Whose AI? Refining the Philippine AI Regulation Act toward a Contextual AI Ethic
abstract: The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) systems in the Philippines has prompted the drafting of the Artificial Intelligence Regulation Act (AIRA), which incorporates internationally recognized principles, such as transparency, accountability, fairness, and risk-based classification. While these principles echo the OECD, UNESCO, and EU AI frameworks, AIRA assumes that universalist ethical safeguards can be adapted unchanged into a context marked by deep socioeconomic inequality, pervasive digital divides, and a fragmented governance landscape. Empirical evidence shows that poverty, inadequate primary education outcomes, and precarious “digital sweatshop” labor conditions limit the capacity of Filipino stakeholders to benefit from procedural safeguards alone. This paper argues that AIRA must be reoriented toward a relational, virtue-based ethic rooted in Filipino concepts of loób (interior moral self) and kapwa (shared self), which foreground empathy, communal responsibility, and the Filipino notion of katarungan (justice).
